title: Antigens: Definition, Properties, and Immunogenicity
subtitle: Epitopes, haptens, antigen classes, adjuvants, and superantigens.
author: Tikrit University · College of Medicine · Microbiology Department

blocks.text: An antigen is a substance specifically recognized by antibodies or lymphocyte receptors. An immunogen induces an immune response. Antigenicity is the capacity for specific binding; immunogenicity is the capacity to induce humoral or cell-mediated immunity. An epitope is the particular molecular region recognized by an antibody, B-cell receptor, or T-cell receptor.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Explain B-cell and T-cell epitope recognition
Classify antigens by source, chemical nature, completeness, and lymphocyte dependence
Analyze the molecular, host, processing, and exposure factors that control immunogenicity

blocks.title: From antigen structure to lymphocyte recognition

steps.title: Molecular structure
steps.description: An antigen contains one or more epitopes.

steps.title: Accessibility or processing
steps.description: B-cell determinants remain accessible; T-cell determinants are released as peptides.

steps.title: Specific receptor binding
steps.description: BCR, antibody, or TCR binds its matching determinant.

steps.title: Activation context
steps.description: Costimulation, host genetics, dose, route, and adjuvant signals shape the response.

blocks.text: A complete antigen is both antigenic and immunogenic. A hapten is antigenic but too small to induce a response alone. Covalent or stable association with a larger carrier provides helper determinants and converts the complex into an effective immunogen. Penicillin and other drugs may behave as haptens after binding host proteins, producing drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Hapten and carrier
blocks.alt: Diagram showing a hapten coupled to a carrier molecule.
blocks.caption: A hapten gains immunogenicity after linkage to a larger carrier.

blocks.title: Classification by source
rows: Normal self component recognized by an autoimmune response
Differs among members of the same species

blocks.title: Classification by chemical nature
rows: Usually highly immunogenic because of size and structural complexity
Can be immunogenic and may activate B cells without conventional T-cell help
Usually weak alone; recognition can depend on association and presentation context
Usually weak alone; immunogenicity rises in complexes or abnormal contexts

blocks.title: T-dependent and T-independent antigens
rows: Not required for initial B-cell activation
Some responses are limited in young children

blocks.title: Molecular and processing factors
rows: Greater difference from self generally increases immunogenicity
Larger molecules are generally more immunogenic
Proteins and structurally complex molecules provide more determinants
Particulate or aggregated material is often more immunogenic than highly soluble material
Shared and species-restricted structures affect recognition
Some antigens are associated with particular tissues or organs
Material must be processed appropriately for many T-cell responses
Number, accessibility, and similarity of determinants shape response strength and specificity

blocks.title: Host and exposure factors
rows: MHC alleles and other immune-response genes alter presentation and responsiveness
Very low or very high doses may be less effective or induce tolerance
Subcutaneous or intramuscular exposure favors systemic responses; mucosal exposure can favor IgA
Repeated exposure and boosters strengthen memory responses
Immaturity, aging, disease, and immunosuppression alter responsiveness
Existing antibody can suppress response by rapidly clearing antigen
Allergen exposure can favor IgE-mediated responses in susceptible hosts

blocks.title: Applied examples
rows: Injection site, dose, and schedule affect the response
Reactivates memory and strengthens the secondary response
Supports secretory IgA at mucosal surfaces
Anti-D immunoglobulin after an Rh-positive infant
Preformed antibody clears Rh antigen and prevents sensitization of an Rh-negative mother

blocks.text: An adjuvant is administered with an antigen to enhance immunogenicity without becoming the target of the specific response.

steps.title: Antigen persistence
steps.description: A depot or retained antigen prolongs exposure.

steps.title: Innate activation
steps.description: Microbial or particulate signals activate local innate cells.

steps.title: Antigen uptake and presentation
steps.description: Antigen-presenting cells capture and process antigen more efficiently.

steps.title: Costimulation and cytokines
steps.description: Activated antigen-presenting cells provide stronger lymphocyte signals.

blocks.title: Adjuvant examples
rows: Common vaccine adjuvant that promotes local antigen uptake and innate activation
Experimental water-in-oil preparation; complete form contains mycobacterial products
Live attenuated mycobacterial stimulus used in selected immune applications

blocks.text: A superantigen cross-links MHC class II and selected T-cell receptor Vβ regions outside the conventional peptide-binding groove. The interaction activates a large polyclonal T-cell population, causing massive cytokine release followed by dysfunction, anergy, or apoptosis.

blocks.title: Superantigen-driven T-cell activation
blocks.description: Trace nonconventional receptor cross-linking to systemic inflammation.

steps.title: MHC II binding
steps.description: The superantigen binds the outer surface of MHC class II without conventional peptide processing.

steps.title: TCR Vβ cross-linking
steps.description: The molecule simultaneously engages selected TCR Vβ families.

steps.title: Polyclonal activation
steps.description: Many unrelated T-cell clones become activated.

steps.title: Cytokine surge
steps.description: Activated T cells and antigen-presenting cells release large quantities of cytokines.

steps.title: Systemic effects
steps.description: Fever, inflammation, shock, followed by immune dysfunction, anergy, or apoptosis may occur.

exam.title: Antigens and immunogenicity exam
exam.instructions: Answer every question. Submit once to receive a score, correct answers, and explanations.

questions.prompt: Which term means the capacity to induce an immune response?
questions.explanation: Immunogenicity is the ability to induce humoral or cell-mediated immunity.

questions.prompt: The discrete region recognized by an antibody or receptor is an _____.
questions.explanation: An epitope is an antigenic determinant.

questions.prompt: How do T cells usually recognize antigen?
How many major factors influencing immunogenicity are enumerated?
questions.explanation: Twelve factors are identified, from foreignness through dose, route, and exposure pattern.

pairs.right: Different member of the same species

questions.explanation: These classifications describe origin or biological relationship.

questions.history: A patient develops hypersensitivity after a small drug molecule binds covalently to host protein.
questions.prompt: What role did the drug play?
questions.explanation: A small drug can become immunogenic after binding a carrier protein.

questions.prompt: Which response is typical of a T-independent antigen?
questions.explanation: T-independent antigens generally cause IgM-dominant responses with limited memory.

questions.prompt: A molecule that enhances the response to a coadministered antigen is an _____.
Match adjuvant mechanisms to their effects.

questions.history: An Rh-negative mother receives anti-D immunoglobulin after delivering an Rh-positive infant.
options: Clear fetal Rh antigen before maternal sensitization
Convert Rh antigen into a hapten
questions.explanation: Preformed antibody suppresses sensitization by clearing antigen.

questions.prompt: Where does a superantigen bind MHC class II?
options: Inside the conventional peptide groove only
questions.explanation: Superantigens bind the outer surface of MHC II.

questions.prompt: Superantigens engage selected T-cell receptor _____ regions.
questions.explanation: TCR Vβ engagement drives broad clone activation.

questions.prompt: Match each superantigen source to an example.

questions.history: A patient has high fever, hypotension, and diffuse inflammation caused by simultaneous activation of many unrelated T-cell clones.
questions.prompt: Which mechanism best explains the syndrome?
options: Superantigen cross-linking of MHC II and TCR Vβ
questions.explanation: Broad Vβ engagement produces polyclonal activation and a cytokine surge.

questions.prompt: Which molecular property generally increases immunogenicity?
questions.explanation: Large, foreign, complex, processable molecules tend to be more immunogenic.

questions.prompt: How many broad chemical antigen classes are listed?
questions.explanation: Proteins, polysaccharides, lipids, and nucleic acids are listed.

questions.prompt: A repeated vaccine exposure that strengthens memory is a _____ dose.

questions.explanation: These distinctions define the major recognition and completeness categories.
